name: Dopamine detox

image.caption: Valley Spring Recovery Center Featured Image Template - Dopamine: Definition, Function, Production, Release, and Detox

lead: A dopamine detox means pulling back from stimulating habits such as social media, gaming, junk food and pornography for a set period. In ascension circles it is used to regain focus and motivation so gym, grooming and study routines get done, sometimes alongside no-masturbation challenges.

It was popularised in 2019 by psychologist Cameron Sepah as a behavioural tool for compulsive habits, and he has said the name is misleading since the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not lower dopamine. Neuroscientists say dopamine drives motivation and learning and cannot be reset by avoiding stimuli. No large trials test it directly; related reviews of social-media detoxes report a small reduction in depressive symptoms.

paras: People set a period, from a day to a few weeks, in which they cut phones, social media, gaming, junk food or porn, and fill the time with exercise, reading or study. Some forum users report feeling focused afterward, while others report feeling flat.

Extreme versions may worsen anxiety, loneliness or restrictive habits, and the practice is not a treatment for addiction or depression. Some people describe withdrawal-like symptoms when quitting substances alongside it.

angle.text: Ascension circles use temporary abstinence from stimulating activities to regain motivation for gym, grooming and study routines. The idea that it resets brain chemistry is disputed by neuroscientists, and no appearance outcomes have been tested.

lead: A dopamine detox, also called dopamine fasting, is a wellness practice of temporarily abstaining from pleasurable or stimulating activities such as social media, gaming, junk food, shopping and pornography [1][2]. It was popularised in 2019 by California psychologist Cameron Sepah, who framed it as a cognitive behavioural tool for compulsive behaviours [1].

Sepah has said the name is misleading and that the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviour, not to lower dopamine itself [1]. Neuroscientists and health commentators have criticised the framing, noting that dopamine is involved in motivation, learning and reward prediction [1][2]. No large randomised trials have tested dopamine fasting directly [2].
On looksmax.org the idea appears in threads promoting it as a productivity or motivation reset, and in threads where users report disappointing results [3][4].
infobox: Social media, gaming, junk food, pornography

paras: Wikipedia credits Sepah with developing the practice and naming it, and describes it as drawing on stimulus-control methods from CBT [1]. Grokipedia states it spread through Silicon Valley circles, social media and productivity podcasts and peaked during the 2020 lockdowns [2]. Media coverage in 2019, including The New York Times and Vice, treated it as a Silicon Valley wellness trend [1].

Definitions vary. Some versions limit it to online technology, while others extend to work, exercise, conversation and physical contact; an extreme version is sensory deprivation [1]. Sepah's framework uses graduated fasts at daily, weekly, quarterly and yearly intervals, and psychiatrist Anna Lembke has endorsed a 24-hour phone-free fast as a starting point [2].

A looksmax.org post describes a seven-day reduction of social media, no phone in the bedroom and replacing stimulation with exercise, reading and sunlight, and says it is not about cutting out dopamine itself [3].

No studies found testing dopamine fasting itself. Related work includes a 2024 meta-analysis of social-media detox interventions (about 10 studies, roughly 2,500 participants) that found a small reduction in depressive symptoms but no significant effects on life satisfaction, stress or overall well-being [2]. A 2018 review by Christopher Ferguson reported that technology use raises dopamine far less than drugs of abuse and found no conclusive evidence that it desensitises the brain [1].

Critics including Harvard Health's Peter Grinspoon have called it a fad built on misunderstood science, while saying Sepah's approach is sensible if not new [1]. Neuroscientist Ciara McCabe has disputed the idea that the brain can be reset by short-term avoidance [1]. Grokipedia states any benefits are more plausibly due to behaviour change, habituation or placebo effects [2].

Extreme versions may worsen anxiety, loneliness or restrictive patterns, and it is not a treatment for addiction or depression; people with ADHD or substance use disorders are advised to consult a professional first [2].

It is grouped with 'motivationmaxxing' and no-masturbation challenges. One looksmax.org user reported that a week of cutting out social media and music left everything feeling bland, and another user replied that it is comparable to no-masturbation challenges [4].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the dopamine detox is presented as a motivation and focus reset, with some users reporting benefits and others reporting flat mood afterwards [3][4].
